newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Key ministers survive S.Korean cabinet shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Key ministers survive S.Korean cabinet shake-up.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam reshuffled his cabinet on Tuesday but kept his foreign, defence and key economic ministers in what opposition politicians described as a game of musical chairs.
The president also retained Prime Minister Koh Kun in the shakeout which affected half the 22-member cabinet.

"This reshuffle reflects President Kim's intention to pursue economic and securities policies effectively, while managing December presidential elections in a strict, fair manner," presidential spokesman Yoon Yeo-joon told reporters.
Government officials said Kim kept ministers responsible for foreign and security policies ahead of crucial four-nation talks involving the two Koreas, the United States and China.

Senior officials from the four countries are due to meet in New York later on Tuesday to set an agenda and other procedural details for talks aimed at hammering out a lasting peace on the Korean peninsula by replacing the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a treaty.

The spokesman said seven of those dropped from the cabinet were members of the ruling New Korea Party. They were the ministers for agriculture, environment, health and welfare, maritime affairs and government administration as well as two political affairs ministers.
Home Affairs Minister Kang Oon-tae was replaced by former government administration minister Cho Hae-nyoung, and Justice Minister Choi Sang-yup by state prosecutor Kim Jong-koo.
Political analysts and opposition parties described Tuesday's move as a game of musical chairs, saying the new home affairs and justice minister were drawn from the government.
"No new appointees are independent figures. They are the ones who have toed Kim's line," said spokeswoman Park Sun-suck of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
Lee Jung-bock, who lectures on politics at Seoul National University, called the shakeout "a public relations stunt".
"The new ministers won't even have time to adjust to their new posts. They won't be able to function," said Lee. "If you believe it's for fair elections, then you're being duped."

Lee Ki-tak, who lectures at Yonsei University, said Kim was demonstrating his tendency to make major decisions by himself and not give enough time for ministers to take responsibility for major policies.
"He has reshuffled the cabinet so many times," he said. Koh, appointed in March, is the sixth premier during the president's 4-1/2 years in office.
Kim retained Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik despite the fact that he is a member of the ruling party. Kang said he would quit the party soon.
Kang and Trade, Industry and Energy Minister Lim Chang-yeul stayed in the cabinet as the president wanted continuity in current economic policies, Kim's aide said.
South Korea has pledged to press ahead with reforms to introduce greater competition and modernise the financial industry despite financial woes involving some major industrial conglomerates.

Other cabinet ministers sacked on Tuesday are Labour Minister Jin Nyum and Education Minister Ahn Byung-young. Jin was succeeded by economic technocrat Lee Ki-ho and Ahn by philosophy professor Lee Myung-hyun.
